Full text

Abstract

Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) prompts participants to report on their current emotions, cognitions, or behaviors multiple times per day across several days, yielding rich, high-frequency data. However, the high frequency of measurement can burden participants, leading to disengagement in the form of non-compliance or careless/insufficient effort responding (C/IER), which compromises the validity of conclusions drawn from EMA data. To minimize these effects, it is crucial to understand how EMA design factors influence respondent disengagement. This study investigates how response format, a comparatively subtle design choice, affects C/IER as an important but hard-to-detect aspect of disengagement. We re-analyzed data from two experimental EMA studies, in which surveys were administered either in a Likert or a visual analogue scale (VAS) format in between-subjects designs. Each dataset was analyzed with one of two state-of-the-art confirmatory mixture modeling approaches to examine whether response format affects (a) the overall level of C/IER and (b) its associations with two fatigue-and attention-related contextual factors: the cumulative number of EMA study days and time of day. Across datasets and analytical approaches, we found indications that Likert scales yield up to 3 percentage points higher rates of C/IER than VASs, though the temporal patterns varied across studies. In Study I, differences were observed in overall C/IER levels, with parallel increases across EMA days. In Study II, initial C/IER was comparable between formats, but the Likert format showed a steeper increase over time. Implications for EMA design are discussed.

[div-01]

In ecological momentary assessment (EMA), participants report on variables such as their current emotions or behaviors multiple times per day over multiple days. EMA has gained traction in psychological research for capturing within-person dynamics (Hamaker & Wichers, 2017) and how psychological experiences are shaped by context (Mestdagh & Dejonckheere, 2021; Myin-Germeys et al., 2018). However, the intensive nature of EMA protocols can impose substantial burden on participants (Eisele et al., 2022), and participants may respond by becoming increasingly disengaged. This can manifest as failing to respond to scheduled assessments (non-compliance) or, if responding, doing so hastily and with limited regard for item content (careless or insufficient effort responding; C/IER), producing responses that do not reflect the variables being measured and compromising the validity of conclusions drawn from EMA data. This issue has motivated research into how EMA protocols can be designed to reduce participant burden and the disengaged behaviors that result from it (Businelle et al., 2024; Conner & Reid, 2012; Eisele et al., 2022; Hasselhorn et al., 2022; McCarthy et al., 2015; Reiter et al., 2025; Ulitzsch et al., 2025; Walsh & Brinker, 2016). Most of this work has focused on design features closely tied to the substantive research question, such as questionnaire length or the number of prompts per day (but see Businelle et al., 2024; Reiter et al., 2025, for investigations of more subtle design choices). This means that adhering to design recommendations derived from these studies can sometimes constrain or alter what is, or can be, studied; for example, changing the timing or spacing of prompts may affect which temporal dynamics can be meaningfully examined or alter the interpretation of (cross-)lagged effects. In addition, this line of research has focused primarily on non-compliance (Businelle et al., 2024; Conner & Reid, 2012; McCarthy et al., 2015; Reiter et al., 2025; Walsh & Brinker, 2016), while the effects of EMA design choices on C/IER are less well understood (but see Eisele et al., 2022; Hasselhorn et al., 2022; Ulitzsch et al., 2025).

The present study extends this line of research in two ways: First, focusing on Likert and visual analogue scales (VASs)-arguably the two most commonly employed response formats in EMA-we examine the effect of response format on disengagement in EMA. Response format can often be varied without interfering with the core research question. Previous studies conducted in EMA contexts did not find response-format differences in psychometric properties or substantive conclusions, aside from minor differences in within-person variability as well as higher correlations with external (clinical) criteria and reduced floor effects for VASs (Haslbeck et al., 2025; Vollbracht et al., 2026). With respect to disengagement specifically, these studies also found no response-format differences in compliance; however, initial evidence from a cross-sectional study using computer-based questionnaires suggests that VASs may elicit more C/IER than Likert scales (Zhang, Domingue, et al., 2025). While it is not clear that this cross-sectional evidence extends to EMA, careful selection of the response format may reduce C/IER without substantially altering planned research designs (see Ulitzsch, Buchholz, et al., 2024, for related arguments in cross-sectional survey design).

Second, we shift attention to C/IER as a harder-to-detect form of disengagement compared to non-compliance. With research on how to best measure this behavior in EMA still in its infancy, the present study hence also serves to showcase how two recently developed model-based approaches (Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al., 2024; Vogelsmeier et al., 2024) can be used to (a) identify instances of C/IER, (b) investigate transitions between attentive responding and C/IER, and (c) examine its contextual correlates such as study day progression and time of day. To investigate response-format differences in C/IER, we re-analyze two EMA datasets with experimentally varied response format, each using one of the two analysis approaches. Before turning to these analyses, we briefly review the literature on the identification of C/IER in EMA to motivate our methodological choices.

Identifying C/IER in EMA

Following the cross-sectional survey literature, we define C/IER as "a response set in which the respondent answers a survey measure with low or little motivation to comply with survey instructions, correctly interpret item content, and provide accurate responses" (Huang et al., 2012, p.100), as distinct from attentive responding, where responses reflect the variables to be measured.

A growing body of research has addressed the detection of C/IER in EMA, yet no consensus has emerged on best practices, nor is one likely to: (a) C/IER is inherently unobservable, so no ground truth exists against which to establish universally optimal methods, and (b), more importantly, the best-suited method may differ across EMA studies, as a method effective in one setting may rely on assumptions or data characteristics absent in another.

Broadly, existing methods can be divided into four categories. First, researchers may ask participants to self-report on momentary C/IER (as used in Eisele et al., 2022), though this rests on the peculiar assumption that respondents exhibiting C/IER on content items nonetheless provided attentive, valid responses when reporting on their behavior. Second, researchers may administer attention checks (e.g., instructing participants to select a specific response option; also used in Eisele et al., 2022); however, these are generally recommended to be used sparingly (Meade & Craig, 2012), yielding limited and potentially underpowered measures of C/IER. Third, researchers may derive behavioral indicators from item response and/or collateral data that may signal C/IER (see Hasselhorn et al., 2023; Jaso et al., 2022). Common examples include inconsistent responses to psychometric antonyms (e.g., reporting being both stressed and relaxed) or unrealistically short response times (see, e.g., Revol et al., 2024, for an example of recent preprocessing guidelines). Although widely used in practice, these methods involve a high number of researcher degrees of freedom and lack strong theoretical guidance, both in how indicators are constructed and in setting thresholds for distinguishing attentive from C/IER observations. These largely arbitrary decisions can substantially alter conclusions about the prevalence of C/IER (see, e.g., Niessen et al., 2016; Ulitzsch, Pohl, et al., 2022, for cross-sectional; and Vogelsmeier, Siepe, et al., 2025, for EMA demonstrations).

Finally, researchers may draw on recently developed confirmatory mixture models (Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al., 2024; Vogelsmeier et al., 2024), which we adopt here. These models assume observations stem from one of a set of a priori specified response states-in our case, an attentive state or a C/IER state. State membership is unobserved; however, each state is assumed to correspond to a distinct data-generating process. As discussed below, subject-matter theories about these processes are incorporated through constraints on state-specific measurement models. In EMA, such models have been formulated for both item response data from multi-item scales (Vogelsmeier et al., 2024) and collateral screen-time data (i.e., time required to complete the EMA survey; Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al., 2024)

The Present Study

The present study pursues two complementary aims. Substantively, it explores how response format as a subtle design choice impacts C/IER occurrence in EMA. Methodologically, it demonstrates how different recently developed confirmatory mixture modeling approaches can be used to study C/IER in EMA data, highlighting their respective strengths and limitations.

To this end, we analyze two experimental datasets, each employing a between-subjects design in which EMA surveys were administered either in a Likert or a VAS format, and, respectively, employ one of two confirmatory mixture modeling approaches (Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al., 2024; Vogelsmeier et al., 2024) to address the following research questions: RQ1. Does response format affect the overall level of C/IER in EMA? RQ2. Do associations between C/IER and two major fatigue-and attention-related contextual correlates-(a) the cumulative number of completed EMA days and (b) time of day-differ across response formats? In other words, is one response format better suited to buffer potential fatigue effects arising from repeated survey completion and/or to maintain participant attentiveness across the day? Addressing these research questions requires analytical approaches that are best suited to the specific data scenarios. The two confirmatory mixture modeling approaches used in this study share common conceptual foundations but differ in their data requirements and practical applicability. The method for item response data from multi-item scales proposed by Vogelsmeier et al. (2024) requires responses from an (ideally well-established) multi-item scale with known dimensionality. When scales are short, as is often the case in EMA, it further requires items to be worded in different directions to produce trustworthy conclusions (Uglanova et al., 2025b). These conditions were met in only one of the two EMA datasets included in the present study (Study I).

In contrast, the approach based on collateral screen-time information proposed by Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al. (2024) does not rely on these requirements and is therefore more general: it can be applied whenever screen times are available for a set of items administered at each measurement occasion.

However, it is computationally more demanding and more prone to convergence issues (Vogelsmeier, Siepe, et al., 2025). Indeed, although adequate screen-time data were available for both datasets, the model converged successfully for only one of them (Study II).

Rather than presenting the two datasets in separate empirical studies, the present study intentionally combines evidence from two EMA datasets that differ in both data characteristics and analytical approach. While the confounding between dataset and analytical approach across the two studies precludes determining whether differences in conclusions stem from specific characteristics of the empirical studies or from differences in the sensitivity of the two analytical approaches to particular behavioral patterns, the joint consideration of both studies enables us to initiate cumulative efforts to understand response-format effects on C/IER and to triangulate results across complementary methodological perspectives.

Study I: Comparing Momentary C/IER on a Four-Item Pleasant-Unpleasant

Mood Scale with a Mixture IRT Approach

Data for Study I originate from Vollbracht et al. (2026) and were initially collected to investigate differences in psychometric properties as well as to assess measurement invariance across response formats. The EMA study by Vollbracht et al. (2026) included several multi-item scales.

Here, we focus on one four-item scale that was administered at every measurement occasion and contained both positively and negatively worded items, making it well-suited for examining C/IER using the mixture IRT approach by Vogelsmeier et al. (2024). Vollbracht et al. (2026) also recorded response times for each item response (defined as the time elapsed between item presentation and the respondent clicking the "next" button), which allowed us to reconstruct the total time spent on the four items. Analyses of these timing data using the screen-time-based approach by Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al. (2024) did not converge; therefore, for Study I, we report only results on identifying C/IER from item responses. We do, however, use the times spent on the four mood items to relate them to the uncovered response states to aid their interpretation.

Data

Participants (age 18 to 68 years, M = 27.4, SD = 9.2; 78% female, 21% male, 1% other) were randomly assigned to either the Likert scale or the VAS group. The data analyzed for the present study comprised 10,640 measurement occasions nested in 200 participants for the Likert group, and 11,089 occasions nested in 206 participants for the VAS group. Of 84 possible measurement occasions, participants completed 53 on average in the Likert group and 54 in the VAS group (63% and 64%, respectively). At each measurement occasion, pleasant-unpleasant mood was assessed with an adapted short version of the Multidimensional Mood Questionnaire (Steyer et al., 1997), which has been used in previous EMA studies (e.g., Lischetzke et al., 2012 Lischetzke et al., , 2022)).

Participants indicated how they felt "just now (right before the prompt)" on four bipolar items: unwell/well, good/bad (reverse-scored), dissatisfied/satisfied, and happy/unhappy (reverse-scored).

For the VAS, only the extremes were labeled and numbered with -50 and 50, respectively. The display had no ticks or start position. For the employed five-point Likert scale, all response options were numbered from -2 to 2, and extremes were labeled. For a visualization, see

Data Analysis Approach

To compare response behavior and its contextual correlates across Likert and VAS formats, we use the confirmatory mixture IRT approach for intensive longitudinal data by Vogelsmeier et al. (2024), which is based on mixture IRT component models that have originally been developed to identify C/IER in cross-sectional data (see, e.g., Jin et al., 2018; Uglanova et al., 2025b; Ulitzsch, Pohl, et al., 2022 , 2023; Ulitzsch, Yildirim-Erbasli, et al., 2022; Ulitzsch et al., 2020; van Laar & Braeken, 2022). Attentive responses are assumed to follow a regular IRT model. Response patterns that deviate from the attentive model specification and presumably go back to C/IER are captured by one or more residual states. The number of residual states is determined based on model selection criteria and interpretability. Each observation is probabilistically assigned to the state it most likely belongs to. This part of the model addresses RQ1. Transition dynamics among these states alongside their person-level and contextual correlates are investigated with a latent Markov model (LMM; e.g., Bartolucci et al., 2014) and form the basis for addressing RQ2. The technical details are provided in the following sections.

Data structure

We denote by y ijt the response of participant i ∈ {1, . . . , N } to item j ∈ {1, . . . , J} at measurement occasion t ∈ {1, . . . , T }. In the present study, the J items are assumed to measure a common substantive momentary state and use G + 1 ordered response categories. For Likert items, the number of categories corresponds directly to the number of available response options. For VAS items, the continuous response scale is discretized by dividing it into G +1 = 10 equally spaced bins. 1 In Appendix A, we provide a simulation study investigating the accuracy of inferences about C/IER based on discretized continuous, bounded VAS data, contextualized against performance of the approach with five-point Likert data. To this end, we generated data using either a confirmatory mixture model for continuous, bounded VAS responses (Zhang, Domingue, et al., 2025) (with responses subsequently discretized into 10 categories) or a mixture model for discrete, 1 In preliminary analyses, we examined a simplified version of the Bayesian Beta mixture IRT model for VAS data described by Zhang, Domingue, et al. (2025), replacing the person-specific attentiveness probability with a single global parameter. Despite this simplification, the model failed to converge even with a large number of iterations, indicating that the data set may have been too large to achieve convergence in a reasonable time. ordered responses, as employed here, but analyzed all data using the latter (i.e., the mixture model for discrete, ordered responses). Our results indicate that this approach yields accurate estimates of mixture proportions and high specificity of individual attentiveness classifications, whereas sensitivity was lower for VAS data, particularly under uniform random responding. Notably, accurate estimation of mixture proportions includes conditions simulating midpoint responding, for which the two response formats differed considerably in their empirical prevalence, as discussed below. For other types of residual response patterns, however, the analysis model was challenged differently depending on response format, such that observed differences between response formats could partly reflect statistical artifacts rather than genuine differences in residual-state prevalence.

Appendix C further provides sensitivity analyses to assess the dependency of conclusions on the chosen number of bins. Results remained largely consistent when using substantially more bins (G +1 = 15; Cohen's κ = .78 for agreement in modal state assignment with the main analysis) but showed some differences with fewer bins (G +1 = 5; κ = .54), suggesting that a discretization into G +1 = 10 bins was likely sufficiently sensitive to approximate the distribution of VAS data for the purpose of detecting C/IER.

The number of time points T may vary across individuals; however, for simplicity, we omit the participant-specific index and refer to the measurement occasions generically as t = 1, . . . , T.

The responses at each time point are collected in 1 × J vectors y it = (y i1t , . . . , y iJt ), which in turn form the subject-specific T × J data matrices Y i = (y ′ i1 , . . . , y ′ iT ) ′ . These individual matrices are stacked to create the full dataset Y = (Y ′ 1 , . . . , Y ′ N ) ′ , comprising a total of N i=1 T i rows.

Measurement models

We assume that at each measurement occasion t, participant i can be in one of K + 1 latent states k ∈ {1, 2, . . . , K + 1}, with one representing an attentive and the remaining K representing residual states. 2 Note that we refer to the states as residual rather than C/IER states because the specific response behavior they capture must be inferred from the state-specific parameter estimates. The state memberships are indicated via the binary indicators s itk . These are equal to 1 for state k and equal to zero for the other states. Specifically, s it1 = 1 denotes an attentive state membership and s it2 = 1, s it3 = 1, . . . , s it,K+1 = 1 denotes membership in one of K residual states that capture response patterns that do not align with the attentive measurement model and potentially stem from C/IER.

Attentive responses are assumed to follow a graded response model (GRM; Samejima, 1969 Samejima, , 2016)). That is, the probability that an attentive participant i selects response option g or higher on item j on measurement occasion t is modeled as where α j gives the loading parameter of item j on the substantive momentary state, θ it gives participant i's location on the substantive state at the tth measurement occasion, and κ 1jg is the gth category threshold for item j.

Note that raw item responses are modeled, i.e., item responses to negatively worded items are not re-coded. Hence, in the case that there are negatively worded items in the administered scales, loading parameters α j can be expected to take negative values.

For model identification, a standard normal distribution is assumed for θ it.

The remaining K states are intended to capture residual response patterns that are unrelated to both the substantive state-reflected in factor loadings constrained to zero-and the item content-reflected in category thresholds constrained to be equal across all items. That is,

Hence, in these states, the model estimates only the marginal category probabilities, which are determined by the shared category thresholds. These probabilities describe typical response patterns of observations where answers deviate from the assumed attentive measurement model.

The K states represent subgroups with distinct marginal category preferences. Typically, such states are assumed to capture C/IER and have in previous research been shown to be capable of "absorbing" a variety of C/IER behavior, ranging from random responding to straight-lining (e.g. Ulitzsch, Pohl, et al., 2022). However, as will be shown below, inspection of the state-specific marginal category probabilities may give rise to alternative interpretations of the phenomena captured by a given state, such that careful inspection of marginal state-specific category preferences is warranted. The number of residual states K is determined by model comparisons using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC; Schwarz, 1978) and considerations regarding substantive interpretability of the resultant residual states.

Transition model

The transition model describes how individuals transition between the attentive and residual states and is obtained using an LMM, which is defined by the initial state, transition, and response probabilities. Together, these form the joint distribution of the observations and states for subject i: probabilities indicate the probabilities of being in state k at timepoint t > 1 conditional on state l ∈ {1, . . . , K + 1} at t -1, and, thus, the probabilities of transitioning between states (or staying in the same one).

These probabilities can depend on covariate values at any timepoint, z it . There are two types of LMMs: The regular so-called discrete-time (DT-)LMM assumes the intervals between measurements, δ ti , to be equal, while these intervals are allowed to differ across time points and individuals in the so-called continuous-time (CT-)LMM (Böckenholt, 2005; Jackson & Sharples, 2002; Vogelsmeier et al., 2019). We use the latter because intervals are unequal in our data. The interval-specific transition probabilities in the CT-LMM, p δ ti ,lk = p δ ti (s itk = 1|s it-1,l = 1, z it ), are collected in the (K + 1) × (K + 1) matrix P δ ti with row sums K+1 k=1 p δ ti ,lk = 1. For additional details, we refer to Vogelsmeier et al. (2019).

For intuitively interpreting the covariate effects, for each covariate, one can compare the transition probabilities for an interval of interest for a low score of interest to the probabilities for a high score of interest, keeping the covariate values for the other predictors equal to their sample means. To complement the examination of study-day and time-of-day effects on transitions, trends in average posterior attentiveness probabilities can be visually compared across the two response-format conditions. This approach addresses not only RQ2 but also RQ1, as the probabilities additionally reveal overall differences in attentiveness.

Estimation

The parameters of the measurement models and transition model are obtained via maximum likelihood estimation. We chose a step-wise estimation approach, in which: ( 1 We note that neither does mirt provide confidence intervals for mixture proportions nor is it possible to obtain confidence intervals for transition probabilities for a given covariate score of interest with lmfa. Although resampling procedures could, in principle, be used to derive such intervals, they introduce additional challenges such as label switching in step 1 and they are computationally infeasible for step 3. We therefore compare response-format differences in uncovered state proportions and in transition patterns only descriptively, without statistical inference.

Results

Model selection

Table 1 provides BIC values for the different measurement models fitted to the Likert and VAS data. Compared to a model assuming the attentive measurement model to hold for all observations, the inclusion of one residual state substantially improved model fit for both response formats. Adding a second residual state further improved fit. Including a third residual state, however, worsened model fit for the VAS data and yielded only minor BIC improvements for the Likert data compared with the substantially larger improvements obtained by adding the first and second residual states. Moreover, one of the three residual states in the Likert model had only 1% of the observations, providing limited justification for retaining this additional state. We therefore selected models with two residual states for both response-format groups.

Table 1 BIC Values for Different Measurement Models Model Likert VAS Attentive only 79,573 141,571 Attentive + one residual state 78,873 140,457 Attentive + two residual states 78,755 140,275 Attentive + three residual states 78,736 140,287 Notes: Selected models are highlighted in bold. VAS: visual analogue scale.

RQ1: Inspecting Identified Response States

Most observations were classified as attentive, accounting for 89.40% in the Likert group and 91.96% in the VAS group. In Appendix B, we provide category characteristic curves implied by the attentive-state measurement model parameter estimates for both response formats. In the Likert group, 7.42% of observations were assigned to residual state 2, and 3.18% to residual state 3.

In the VAS group, 3.48% of observations were assigned to residual state 2 and 4.56% to residual state 3. The overall classification certainty for the attentive state was very high, with an average certainty of 1 (rounded to two decimals) for both the Likert and VAS formats. Classification certainty was considerably lower for the two residual states, with values of 0.68 and 0.76 in the Likert group and 0.87 and 0.85 in the VAS group.

Figure 2

Category probabilities in the two residual states for each response format. Each point along the x-axis represents one of the five response categories for the Likert format or one of the ten bins for the VAS format. The y-axis shows model-implied probabilities derived from state-specific category thresholds κ kg , which are assumed to generalize across all mood items. The proportion of observations assigned to each state under a given response format is reported in brackets in the subfigure headings.

As noted above, the two residual states require inspection of their state-specific estimates before they can be interpreted as representing C/IER. For both response formats, the two residual states were characterized by similar patterns. The first residual state (marginal category probabilities displayed in the left column in Figure 2; state proportions are provided in the subfigure headings) was characterized by a probability of essentially 1 to select the Likert midpoint and keep the VAS slider on or very close to the midpoint of the scale. With only four relatively homogeneous items, selecting the midpoint on all of them is a response pattern that can plausibly reflect both attentive responding (e.g., a stable or momentarily elicited midpoint response style, attentively evaluating the item but favoring the middle of the scale when mapping one's judgment to it Baumgartner & Steenkamp, 2001) and C/IER (e.g., due to straight-lining or overly consistent midpoint selection). Hence, the interpretation of this state remains ambiguous. Note, however, that this behavior was twice as likely with the Likert scale. The second residual state (right column in

Figure 2) was characterized by elevated marginal category probabilities for the outer ends of the scale; specifically, the middle-lower and middle-upper response options, respectively, slider-scale positions. In our opinion, this pattern can more clearly be interpreted as C/IER, reflecting the selection of middle-lower and middle-upper responses without sufficient regard for item content.

This interpretation is further corroborated by implausibly positive correlations between responses to differently worded items for observations assigned to this state (e.g., a correlation of .13 between items assessing feeling well and feeling unhappy in the Likert format, and .24 in the VAS format, compared to -.72 and -.78 for observations assigned to the attentive state). However, given the reduced interpretability of the midpoint residual state, our conclusions regarding differences in attentiveness remain tentative and depend on how the residual states are interpreted. If midpoint selection is assumed to reflect attentive responding, one might conclude that the Likert scale reduced C/IER by approximately 1 percentage point compared to the VAS across the entire EMA period, although the VAS may have been more effective in discouraging midpoint responding.

Alternatively, if both residual states are interpreted as reflecting C/IER, the VAS appears to have yielded contamination rates across the EMA study period roughly 2 percentage points lower than the Likert scale. Note that the results remain descriptive because the methodology does not provide error estimates for formal significance testing.

Exploring screen time distributions associated with the identified response states.

To support the interpretation of the uncovered residual states, Figure 3 displays the distribution of log time spent on the four mood items by response state to which observations were assigned using modal assignment. Generally, distributions associated with the different identified states showed strong overlap. However, for both response formats, the distributions of the two residual states were more right-skewed and contained a larger proportion of observations with very short times spent on the four items. This pattern indicates that at least some of these response patterns were generated in a more rushed manner than those attributed to attentive responding and provides preliminary validity evidence for interpreting these states as, at least in part, capturing behavior that deviates from attentive responding. Distributions of log screen times for the four mood items by response state for each response format. Each distribution represents the total time spent on the four items for observations assigned to the respective response state using modal assignment. Residual response states are labeled according to their characteristic distributional patterns. For reference, log screen times of 1, 2, and 3 correspond to approximately 2.7, 7.4, and 20.1 seconds, respectively.

Interestingly, when comparing the screen-time distributions of the two residual states, a different pattern emerged across response formats. For the Likert scale, a larger share of observations assigned to the outer (as opposed to the midpoint) residual state were aberrantly short and showed screen times that deviated more strongly from those attributed to attentive responding, resulting in a bimodal distribution. The first, lower mode occurred at a log screen time of approximately 1.25, corresponding to about 3.5 seconds. The second mode aligned with the mean of the attentive distribution of log screen times and corresponded to roughly exp(2) ≈ 7.4 seconds.

For the VAS, this pattern was reversed: the midpoint state exhibited a bimodal log screen-time distribution strongly resembling the distribution of log screen times of the Likert outer state, while the outer-state log screen-time distribution was only slightly right-skewed. This suggests that the two types of residual response patterns may reflect different underlying response behaviors depending on the response format: while a preference for the outer response options could be attributed with less ambiguity to rushed C/IER in the Likert scale, a similar interpretation appeared to hold for midpoint preferences for the VAS.

RQ2: Inspecting Correlates of Transitioning

To investigate how attentiveness changes across days and time of day, we examine the LMM estimates, including the covariate-specific transition matrices. Note that prior to estimating the transition model, we excluded three and seven individuals in the Likert and VAS groups, respectively, because these individuals had fewer than the minimum required two measurement occasions. The initial-state probabilities for the Likert and VAS groups (rounded to two decimals) were (0.90, 0.06, 0.05) and (0.93, 0.01, 0.06), respectively, indicating that individuals in both groups had a high probability of starting in the first, and hence, attentive state. This probability was slightly smaller for the Likert group. For the Likert group, both time-varying covariates had significant effects (day: χ 2 (6) = 42.41, p < .001; time of day: χ 2 (6) = 18.67, p < .001). For the VAS group, only day had a significant effect (day: χ 2 (6) = 64.75, p < .001; time of day: χ 2 (6) = 7.16, p = .31). Nevertheless, to facilitate a direct comparison of how covariates relate to transition probabilities, we show the effects of both covariates for both response formats in Table 2.

In our interpretation, we omit the effect of time of day in the VAS group, however. For the interpretation, we focus on the most striking findings, which are highlighted using stronger shades.

Day.

For both groups, the comparison of the transition probabilities when completing the EMA questionnaires at the first day with the probabilities when completing the questionnaires at the last day (while holding the time of day equal to its sample mean) showed that the probabilities of transitioning from the midpoint to the attentive state and from the outer to the attentive state were considerably lower towards the end of participation compared to the beginning, with probabilities dropping sharply for both transitions. Relatedly, for days later in time, the probabilities of staying in the midpoint and outer states increased considerably. These results indicate that it is generally less likely to be in the attentive state toward the end of participation and indicate more response pattern stability towards the end of participation. Moreover, regardless of the day, we find relatively similar patterns for transitions from the attentive state to both residual states (midpoint and outer), as well as for transitions from these states back to the

The value on the left of the arrow represents the transition probability associated with a reasonably low covariate value while holding the other covariate score equal to its sample mean; the value on the right of the arrow indicates the transition probability associated with a reasonably high value while holding the other covariate score equal to its sample mean. attentive state (although for the Likert group, at the beginning of the study, probabilities of transitioning to the attentive state are higher from the outer state and for the VAS group, they are higher for the midpoint state). This similarity in transition patterns suggests that the residual states may indeed reflect similar underlying mechanisms.

Time of day.

For the Likert group, the comparison of the transition probabilities when completing the EMA questionnaires at 9 a.m. with the probabilities when completing the questionnaires at 9 p.m. (while holding the day equal to its sample mean) showed that the probabilities of transitioning from the midpoint state to the attentive state were somewhat higher and of transitioning from the outer to the attentive state much higher in the evening than in the morning. Correspondingly, the probabilities of staying in the midpoint and outer states, as well as transitioning to them from the respective other state, were (somewhat) lower in the evening than in the morning. Moreover, regardless of the time of day, we again find relatively similar patterns for transitions from the attentive state to both residual states (midpoint and outer), as well as for transitions from these states back to the attentive state, further supporting that the residual states may reflect similar underlying mechanisms.

Inspecting within-and between-day trajectories.

To provide further intuition for the uncovered response-format differences, Figure 4 displays trajectories of average posterior attentiveness probabilities within and between EMA study days. To simplify the visualization, time of day is grouped into four bins (<10:00 (bin 1), 10:00-14:00 (bin 2), 14:00-19:00 (bin 3), and >19:00 (bin 4)). As can be seen, the Likert group exhibited lower attentiveness from the onset of the EMA. Across the study, however, attentiveness trajectories largely paralleled each other with a small downward trend; the only exception occurs in the final study week, when the Likert group appeared to show sharper declines in average posterior attentiveness probabilities. Study II: Comparing Momentary C/IER in Single-Item Measures With a Mixture Screen-Time-Based Approach Data for Study II are from Haslbeck et al. (2025) and were originally collected to explore which precludes the use of IRT models to detect C/IER. Instead, in Study II, we employ the screen-time-based confirmatory mixture approach proposed by Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al. (2024). This method uses collateral screen-time information that records how long a participant required to complete the EMA survey at each measurement occasion, and it is agnostic to the specific scale structure of the items included in the survey.

Data

For a detailed description and information on ethical approval, see Haslbeck et al. (2025).

In brief, participants (age 18 to 41 years, M = 21.7, SD = 3.9; 85% female, 12% male) were randomly assigned to either the Likert scale or the VAS group. For the present analyses, to have sufficient information for each respondent to estimate person parameters of the attentive measurement model (see Equation 4 of the observations), binge eating (triggered in roughly 15% of the observations), and craving for food (two items, triggered in roughly 20% of the observations), the vast majority of routed items were follow-ups on specific clinical symptoms (e.g., following up on avoidance of certain memories or cravings to gamble) and were therefore rarely triggered in the study's student sample (below 5% of observations, with 16 items triggered in less than 1% of observations), and (b) maybe even more important, the occurrence of routings did not differ across response formats, we deemed potential deviations from the assumption of cross-observation comparability of screen times to be sufficiently minor to be defensible.

For the VAS, only the extremes were labeled. The display had no ticks, and only when a participant touched the screen did a dot appear. The employed seven-point Likert scale ranged from 1 to 7; extremes were labeled and intermediate options numbered. For a visualization, see normal distribution (i.e., the probability of a survey being triggered in the middle of the time interval was maximized). Four of the six surveys contained the same number of items. However, the first and last surveys of the day contained additional items about sleep and experiences throughout the day. Because of these additional items, screen times obtained from the morning and evening are not comparable with the shorter momentary surveys administered during the rest of the day and are, therefore, excluded from data analysis. This reduces the number of measurement occasions to 2,689 and 2,388 for the Likert and VAS groups, respectively. Each of the four prompts could be answered within a 20-minute window. Push notifications were sent when a survey was triggered, and 12 minutes before the survey expired.

Data Analysis Approach

The screen-time-based mixture model by Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al. (2024) is rooted in the common presumption that differences in timing are indicative of differences in response strategies and behavior (De Boeck & Jeon, 2019; Ulitzsch, Shin, & Lüdtke, 2023), and targets the identification of aberrant screen times, presumably too short to evaluate the displayed content and select suitable responses (Bowling et al., 2021; Jaso et al., 2022). The model assumes two states: one captures screen-time trajectories arising from genuine engagement with the EMA surveys, whereas the other captures deviating, less structured screen times that stem from C/IER and are, on average, shorter than those stemming from attentive responding.

The momentary probability of being in the attentive state is modeled with a psychometric latent response model (Maris, 1995; Ulitzsch et al., 2020) as a function of a respondent's attentiveness and occasion-specific factors that may facilitate or hinder sustained attention. In contrast to the separate IRT-based analyses conducted for Study I, we here analyze data from both response formats jointly and model their effects via the inclusion of a participant-level variable moderating the parameters of the latent-response model (as in Ulitzsch et al., 2025).

Data structure

We denote by t im the time in seconds that participant i ∈ {1, . . . , N } took to complete the EMA survey on their mth completed survey (including the first and last surveys of the day), where m ∈ {1, . . . , M }. The number of surveys that a participant replied to may vary across individuals.

However, again, for notational convenience, we omit the participant-specific index.

Measurement models

We assume that when completing an EMA survey, participants can be either in an attentive or a C/IER state. To facilitate the exposition of the latent response model below, we change notation for the latent state and denote by s im = 1 an attentive, and by s im = 0 a C/IER state.

When a participant is attentive, their log screen times are assumed to be governed by a law-of-practice effect, capturing potential speed-up due to repeated exposure to the same questionnaire and familiarization with the EMA delivery system, inspired by models employed in cognitive psychology to model habituation and learning effects (e.g., Evans et al., 2018; Heathcote et al., 2000). The law-of-practice effect is modeled with an exponential decay function and characterized by a participant-specific initial time expenditure parameter τ 1i , determining the attentive screen time required at the very first measurement occasion, a habitual decay parameter τ²i , determining the speed-up rate as a function of the number of completed surveys,foot_1 and a lower asymptote µ 1 , determining the minimum amount of time required for attentive responding:

Here, σ 2 1 denotes the attentive log screen time residual variance.

C/IER screen times are assumed to be independent of participant and occasion characteristics, stemming from a lognormal distribution with a common mean µ 0 and variance where the constraint µ1 = µ 0 + µ * 1 , with µ * 1 , incorporates the assumption that, on average, C/IER requires less time than attentive responding.

Here, µ * 1 can be interpreted as an offset parameter that determines how much longer it, at minimum, takes to generate an attentive response compared to a careless one. To simplify the model and aid convergence, we set σ 20 = σ 2 1 , corresponding to the assumption that, for a given respondent and measurement occasion, attentive and C/IER screen times are predictable with equal precision.

Note that no information about response format is included in the measurement models.

That is, we make a strict invariance assumption for the attentive and C/IER screen time measurement models. Specifically, we assume that (a) the lower asymptotes describing the minimum time needed for attentive responding, (b) the expected log C/IER time, and (c) the residual variance of screen times are identical across formats. This is a strong assumption and would, for example, be violated if the purely mechanical act of selecting a response required different amounts of time across formats. In the present analysis, however, we consider this assumption defensible. Our judgment is based on condition-specific inspections of the screen-time distributions, which were visually indistinguishable.

Latent response model

The latent response model treats the (unobserved and therefore latent) response status as a binary indicator of a person's general attentiveness, ψ i , or, in other words, their ability to withstand features of the assessment that may induce C/IER. The difficulty of maintaining attentiveness at a given measurement occasion may, in turn, vary as a function of the EMA's response format as well as U contextual correlates z imu . As in Study I, we consider the cumulative number of completed EMA days and the time of day at which the participant began their mth completed survey. Specifically, the latent response model is given by where the function c[i] maps the participant i to their assigned experimental condition.

The latent response model's condition-specific parameters determining attentiveness difficulty (ι c ) capture potential differences in the occurrence of C/IER between experimental conditions when all contextual correlates are at zero (ι 0,c ) as well as in its relationship with the considered contextual correlates (ι u,c ). To investigate whether these parameters are credibly different from each other (addressing RQ2), the difference can be obtained as a derived parameter. Further, trends in average model-implied attentiveness probabilities p(s im = 1) or average posterior attentiveness probabilities can be visually compared across conditions. We here focus on the average posterior attentiveness probabilities 4 to align the display of attentiveness trajectories with Study I. Trajectories of 4 Given screen time t im , these can be obtained as , where f 1 (•) and f 0 (•) denote the probability density functions of the attentive and C/IER screen-time measurement models in Equations 4 and 5.

model-implied attentiveness probabilities are provided in Appendix E.

Estimation

Model parameters are obtained via Bayesian estimation with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques. For prior settings, we follow the recommendations provided in Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al. (2024). We refer the reader to the original article for technical details and simulation-based evaluations of model performance (Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al., 2024). For estimation, we use Stan version 2.19 (Carpenter et al., 2017) via the rstan package version 2.19.3 (Guo et al., 2018). We run two MCMC chains with 50,000 iterations each, using the first half as warm-up. We use the posterior mean (EAP) as the Bayesian point estimate and obtain 95% credible intervals for statistical inference. The R and Stan code is available at OSF (https://osf.io/6eywg).

Results

Inspection of the traceplots and potential scale reduction factor values below 1.10 for all parameters (Gelman & Rubin, 1992; Gelman & Shirley, 2011) indicated convergence and good mixing of the chains.

RQ1: Inspecting response behavior

Across both response formats, participants, and measurement occasions, the average attentiveness probability was .93 (95% credible interval: [.92; .95]), corresponding to an expected overall C/IER rate of 7%.

Across the entire EMA, the average attentiveness probability was credibly higher in the VAS condition (.95 [.94; .96]) than in the Likert condition (.92 [.90; .96]; difference: .03 [.01; .06]). On average, careless participants tended to require exp(µ 0 ) = exp(3.58) [3.52; 3.65] = 35.87 seconds to respond to all items administered. The model-implied expected value of the minimum amount of time required for attentive responding was exp(µ * 1 ) = exp(0.38) [0.28; 0.47] = 1.46 times longer, corresponding to 52.46 seconds in total. Results related to the distribution of person parameters are provided in Appendix D. at the beginning of the EMA (ι 0,Likert = -12.23 [-17.01; -7.58]; ι 0,VAS = -10.76 [-15.69; -6.14]; difference: 1.47 [-4.64; 7.92]).

RQ2: Inspecting within-and between-day trajectories

However, as can be seen from Figure 6, the two conditions exhibited different patterns of declines in attentiveness probabilities across the EMA.

Day.

As illustrated in Figure 6, both conditions exhibited increases in attentiveness difficulty (mirrored by declines in average posterior attentiveness probabilities) across days (ι 1,Likert = 0.46 [0.27, 0.69]; ι 1,VAS = 0.19 [0.00, 0.39]), with the effect being more pronounced in the Likert condition (difference: -0.27 [-0.58, 0.00]). These effects corresponded to minor declines in average posterior attentiveness probabilities in the VAS condition (from .96 on day 1 to .95 on day 14), but substantial declines in the Likert condition (from .97 on day 1 to .85 on day 14).

Time of day.

In Figure 6, time of day is grouped into four bins to simplify the visualization (<13:00 (bin 1), 13:00-15:15 (bin 2), 15:15-17:30 (bin 3), and >17:30 (bin 4)). Due to varying numbers of participants within each bin across days, the plotted curves show unsystematic fluctuations within EMA study days. In neither condition did time of day exhibit a relationship with attentiveness difficulty (ι 2,Likert = -0.07 [-0.36; 0.18]; ι 2,VAS = -0.09 [-0.35; 0.14]; difference: -0.02 [-0.35; 0.33]), i.e., attentiveness difficulty remained stable within EMA study days.

Discussion

Previous studies indicate that visual analogue scale (VAS) and Likert scales can be used interchangeably in ecological momentary assessment (EMA) (Haslbeck et al., 2025; Vollbracht et al., 2026), as suggested by their comparable psychometric properties and relationships with external criteria. Hence, reducing participant burden and, in turn, supporting them to remain attentive can be a major consideration when making response-format decisions. The present study compared the occurrence of careless or insufficient effort responding (C/IER) in EMAs based on either Likert or VAS formats. Specifically, we explored whether response format impacts the overall level of C/IER (RQ1) and moderates its associations with cumulative EMA study days (RQ2a) and time of day (RQ2b). We believe that such explorations are instrumental to the development of guidelines for EMA study designs that improve the validity of the resulting data:

Analyses of two experimental EMA datasets using different model-based approaches for identifying and examining C/IER partially corroborated each other's conclusions. Across datasets, we found (a) that VAS formats yielded a 2-3 percentage-point higher proportion of observations classified as attentive responding and (b) that attentive responding declined over study days but remained relatively stable within days for both formats. Overall, these findings provide initial evidence that Likert scales are associated with a lower capacity to sustain attentiveness in EMA.

All else being equal, VASs may yield somewhat more valid EMA data. However, it remains unclear how these effects unfold over time-whether Likert scales lead to higher C/IER from the outset (as suggested by Study I) or contribute to a faster decline in attentiveness as EMA progresses (as suggested by Study II).

Both studies showed comparable rates and overall less C/IER for the VAS format (RQ1).

These results contrast with initial findings of higher C/IER on VASs in cross-sectional settings reported by Zhang, Domingue, et al. (2025). Several hypotheses may explain this discrepancy, warranting further investigation. First, their within-subject design confounded response format with position and repeated-administration effects, which may have contributed to the observed response-format differences. Second, VAS and Likert implementations may have differed from those used here, although this cannot be verified due to the use of secondary, unpublished materials.

Third, the discrepancy may arise from device effects (e.g., moving a slider may be less burdensome than selecting a response option on a smartphone, and vice versa on a computer). 5 Finally, the differences may be attributable to the assessment context: a VAS may be better suited to brief, in-the-moment EMA assessments, whereas this advantage may disappear or even reverse in longer, cross-sectional surveys completed in a dedicated session.

In Study I, using an IRT approach allowed us to identify distinct behavioral response patterns deviating from the specified attentive measurement model. Across both formats, we found residual states characterized by strong preferences for either the scale midpoint or for middle-outer points. The prevalence of these behaviors differed across response formats: midpoint preferences were more common for the Likert format, corroborating previous cross-sectional findings on response-format differences in midpoint responding (Hasson & Arnetz, 2005; Van Laerhoven et al., 2004).

We found initial support that at least parts of the observations assigned to either residual state may be attributable to C/IER: First, both residual states showed a higher occurrence of unusually short screen times compared with the attentive state, indicating more rushed behavior; although for the VAS, this effect was more pronounced for the outer-preference residual state.

Second, we found comparable transition patterns from and to both residual states across EMA study days, which indicates comparable underlying mechanisms. Third, for the outer-preference residual state, we observed implausibly positive correlations between responses to differently worded items for observations assigned to this state. This pattern is inconsistent with an alternative interpretation of this state as an extreme-response style, under which scale structure would be preserved, and responses to differently worded items would therefore be expected to correlate negatively. For the midpoint residual state, however, it remains unclear whether it is reflective of a midpoint response style in attentive responding or straight-lining around the midpoint under C/IER. It is also possible that the residual states reflect inseparable blends of attentive and careless behaviors, with the relative contributions of each varying over the course of the EMA. Future research could address this issue using mixed-methods studies or by incorporating 5 Although previous studies have established near smartphone-computer comparability (Antoun et al., 2017; Buskirk & Andrus, 2014; Wells et al., 2014), this does not necessarily imply comparable C/IER rates. While indicators related to C/IER were considered in these studies, these were generally indirect (e.g., avoiding the "other" option in a half-open response format; Antoun et al., 2017).

additional data, such as screen times, to help disentangle attentive from careless midpoint responding or outer category preferences, for that matter (Ulitzsch, Pohl, et al., 2023).

Across both studies, we found C/IER to increase over EMA study days (corroborating results from Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al., 2024; Ulitzsch et al., 2025; and consistent with general findings from cognitive psychology concerning the effect of simple and monotonous tasks Jangraw et al., 2023), but to remain relatively stable within individual study days (in contrast to results reported in Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al., 2024; Ulitzsch et al., 2025; Vogelsmeier et al., 2024). However, conclusions regarding response-format differences in the relationship between C/IER and EMA study days (RQ2a) and time of day (RQ2b)-and thus in the temporal C/IER dynamics-differed across studies. Study I suggested that response-format differences in C/IER were present from the outset of the EMA, but that, except for minor effects of time of day for the Likert format (and not the VAS), trajectories across days were largely parallel. In contrast, Study II indicated no initial differences between response formats in eliciting C/IER; however, the Likert format appeared to reduce participants' capacity to sustain attentiveness over EMA study days, resulting in higher C/IER rates by the final day. This pattern suggests that VASs may be better suited to mitigate the C/IER-inducing effects of repeated, high-frequency assessments.

Limitations and Future Directions

We must emphasize the exploratory nature of this study. Because we had no a priori hypotheses regarding our research questions, this work should be viewed as an initial step toward understanding response format as a design factor impacting C/IER behavior. Therefore, we caution against treating our results as definitive and highlight the need for future corroboration.

Additionally, both approaches employed to identify and investigate C/IER rely on strong assumptions, violations of which may lead to erroneous conclusions. The mixture IRT approach assumes a correctly specified attentive measurement model and invariance across both participants and time (Vogelsmeier, Jongerling, & Ulitzsch, 2025; Vogelsmeier et al., 2024), and, as shown in the simulation study in Appendix A, can be challenged by specific C/IER patterns that differ across genuine five-point Likert and discretized 10-bin VAS data. The screen-time-based approach relies on assumptions about attentive screen-time trajectories that have not yet been validated and, as noted above, in the present study also assumes strong invariance in the time required for attentive responding and C/IER across different response formats. We emphasize that it cannot be ruled out that our results are at least partially influenced by violations of these or other assumptions.

Moreover, we emphasize that the response-format effects observed in our general-population samples may not generalize to populations with more limited cognitive or attentional resources, or less experience with smartphones, such as clinical or elderly populations. In these groups, for instance, differences in cognitive demands across response formats may be more pronounced, potentially producing stronger response-format effects, or ease-of-use may differ, leading to different patterns of effects. We therefore consider replicating our study in samples from different target populations an important and promising direction for future research.

Furthermore, an important limitation is that response continuity and response interface were confounded in the present study: the Likert scales involved discrete response categories selected via radio buttons, whereas the VAS used a slider. Importantly, these two features are conceptually separable; for example, a slider interface can also be constrained to a small number of discrete response positions. Thus, differences in C/IER cannot be attributed solely to the continuous versus discrete nature of the response scales, as the response interface may also have contributed. This may also be relevant to the divergence from the cross-sectional findings reported by Zhang, Domingue, et al. (2025).

We note that there are several open methodological questions regarding the employed analysis approaches. First, although the approaches considered in the present study are grounded in subject-matter theory on response behavior, uncertainty remains as to whether the observations they flag indeed originate from C/IER. Moving forward, we therefore see a need to gather validity evidence that supports the interpretation of classifications provided by different approaches. For the approaches considered in the present study, such validation efforts have already begun. In cross-sectional data, mixture IRT models have been shown to be sensitive to experimental conditions designed to elicit or prevent C/IER and to align with alternative C/IER indicators such as attention checks or participants' ability to recognize survey content (Uglanova et al., 2025a). For the screen-time-based approach, Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al. (2024) reported that responses flagged as careless based on timing data were also more likely to display implausible response patterns, such as reporting being relaxed and stressed at the same time. We encourage further work aimed at strengthening the validity evidence for these and other emerging approaches.

Second, approaches capable of perfectly recovering participants' attentiveness statuses will most likely never be developed. We, therefore, strongly recommend triangulating and probing the robustness of conclusions drawn from different approaches (as in Vogelsmeier, Siepe, et al., 2025).

In the present study, a direct comparison was not possible due to convergence issues for the screen-time-based approach in Study I and unsuitability of item response data for the mixture IRT approach in Study II. The approaches, however, yielded similar conclusions across data sets, and in our view provide initial though not definitive support for their robustness. We, nevertheless, acknowledge that the confounding of data set and analysis method is one of the major limitations of the present study, and encourage replications of our analyses with data sets where both models are applicable.

Third, differences in both the direction and magnitude of observed response-format effects on attentiveness across the two studies may partly reflect variations in methodological choices (e.g., different model assumptions and sensitivities to specific aspects of respondent behavior) and data characteristics (e.g., participant rewards). Researchers should keep in mind that this limitation applies not only to the present study but also translates to future studies investigating the effect of scale format on attentiveness in EMA and comparing their results to our findings.

Fourth, while model-based approaches provide useful tools to quantify C/IER and to study its design-based determinants and contextual correlates, handling detected C/IER remains less straightforward. One option is to use posterior state probabilities to filter likely careless responses or to downweight them in subsequent analyses (as discussed in Ulitzsch, Nestler, et al., 2024). This, however, relies on the strong assumption that C/IER is unrelated to respondents' momentary standing on the target construct (e.g., momentary stress or negative affect). If violated, such filtering induces non-ignorable missing values (see Ulitzsch, Domingue, et al., 2023, for related discussions). At the same time, retaining C/IER responses is also problematic, as they contain no information about the target construct. We therefore argue that sensitivity analyses examining the robustness of substantive conclusions across different C/IER handling strategies are particularly important in EMA research, and encourage future research on best practices for handling C/IER once detected.

Finally, future methodological research may develop approaches that integrate the behavioral information contained in EMA item responses and screen times into a unified modeling framework. Drawing inspiration from cross-sectional modeling frameworks (Nagy & Ulitzsch, 2022), this could either be achieved by having mirroring constrained measurement models for item responses and screen times (see Ulitzsch, Pohl, et al., 2022; Zhang, Ulitzsch, & Domingue, 2025, for cross-sectional examples) or by using screen times as predictors of latent states defined by different component models for item responses.

Beyond these limitations, we see our study as part of an emerging line of research examining how subtle design choices can affect respondent behavior in EMA (Businelle et al., 2024; Reiter et al., 2025). We believe that increased attention to such design factors represents a particularly promising direction for future research, as it would support developing guidelines for EMA study design that do not interfere with the substantive research question at hand and that can, as such, be implemented more universally than, say, guidelines concerning questionnaire length.

This can relate to further investigations of response formats, such as the benefits of self-chosen response formats (as in Kutscher & Eid, 2024) or the specifics of implementation of either response format, such as the number of response options (as in Kutscher & Eid, 2020), but also to other design factors such as the specific implementation of reminders or incentives to participate.

For the residual state characterized by uniform random responding, we drew responses from unif(0.01, .99). For the residual state characterized by midpoint responding, observations were drawn from a truncated normal distributions with mean 0.50 and a standard deviation of 0.05. For the residual state with strong slider-position preferences, responses were drawn from one of two truncated normal distributions, each with equal probability, with means 0.20 and 0.80, and a standard deviation of 0.15. Attentive Likert responses were generated according to the GRM displayed in Equation 1.

We set α = (4.00, -5.00, 4.00, -4.00), κ11 = κ13 = (8.00, 5.00, 2.00, -3.00), and κ12 = κ14 = (4.00, -2.00, -6.00, -10.00). For uniform random responding, we drew responses from a uniform discrete distribution. Under midpoint responding, all responses were deterministically set to the middle response category (2). Strong category preferences were simulated by randomly assigning each respondent to one of two response centers, category 1 or category 3. Responses were then drawn from a two-category distribution, where the assigned center received probability .80, while the neighboring category, i.e., the category below for a center of 1, or the category above for a center of 3, received the remaining probability of .20.

We generated 50 datasets for each of the six conditions per response format. We applied a confirmatory mixture IRT model with one residual state to each dataset, with 20 sets of random starting values per replication.

Results concerning the accuracy of identifying observations belonging to the simulated residual state are displayed in Table A1. Under a residual state characterized by midpoint responding, convergence was challenged for both Likert and VAS response formats, with convergence rates ranging from as low as .54 to .92 across replications; a replication was considered non-converged if none of the 20 random starts met the convergence criterion after 1,000 iterations.

Replications that did converge, however, yielded estimates of the proportion of the residual state that were unbiased and exhibited low variability.

Under uniform responding and observation-specific preferences for the outer ends of the scale, convergence was achieved in all replications for both response formats. However, the analysis model was challenged differently by these two types of residual patterns depending on the data-generating response format. For the Likert response format, estimates of the proportion of the residual state were unbiased and exhibited low variability under uniform random responding, but were upwards biased under observation-specific preferences for the outer ends of the scale, especially when the true proportion was below .20. While estimates were unbiased for the larger proportion, they exhibited a markedly higher variability. For the VAS format, the pattern of results for uniform and preference-based responding was partially reversed: under preferences for the outer ends of the scale, the proportion of the residual state was estimated with less or comparable bias than for Likert data, except at the largest proportion. Variability was low throughout, except for an increase at the largest residual-state proportion comparable to the Likert format. When residual-state observations exhibited uniform random responding, in contrast, state proportion estimates showed a downward bias that increased with the size of the residual state, although less than proportionally.

Across data-generating conditions, sensitivity was lower for the VAS than for the Likert format, but both formats showed comparable patterns across conditions. For midpoint and preference-based responding, sensitivity was excellent for the Likert format (1.00, except for preference-based responding at a proportion of .20: .882) and satisfactory for the VAS format (above .80, except for midpoint responding at a proportion of .10: .775). Under uniform responding, sensitivity was markedly lower for both formats and decreased as the proportion of the residual state became smaller, reaching .680 (Likert) and .474 (VAS) at a proportion of .05. Specificity was above .95 for both formats across all conditions.

Based on these results, we conclude that discretized VAS data are not at a general disadvantage compared to Likert data concerning inferences about the proportion of residual states, although observation-level classification was less sensitive for VAS data. This is particularly notable for midpoint responding, which, in Study I, exhibited a comparatively large difference in occurrence across response formats: here, the employed data analysis model yielded accurate conclusions about residual-state proportions regardless of format. Nevertheless, under the other residual patterns, the model was challenged in both the five-point Likert format and the VAS format discretized into 10 categories, but by different patterns, with bias in opposite directions: residual-state proportions were overestimated for Likert data under preference-based responding and underestimated for VAS data under uniform responding.

Hence, it cannot be ruled out that empirical differences between formats stem in part from statistical artifacts rather than genuine differences in the size of residual states.

Note that our simulation study focused exclusively on the impact of VAS discretization on the ability to disentangle different response behaviors. While we found this aspect to be largely unaffected, we emphasize that other parameters not targeted in the present study-such as estimates of the latent state-may be more sensitive to discretization and warrant further investigation before being studied with models applied to discretized VAS data.

Appendix A Simulation Study: Consequences of Discretized Visual Analogue Scales

In our evaluations of the consequences of discretizing VAS data, we focused on the accuracy of identifying observations belonging to a residual state, which is a key prerequisite for subsequent analyses that serve to get a better understanding of participant and occasion characteristics associated with transitioning among attentive and residual states. Results for the discretized VAS data were contextualized against corresponding analyses for data from a five-point Likert scale, where the data-generating model and data analysis model both corresponded to the confirmatory mixture GRM with one residual state defined by Equations 1 and 2.

For both response formats, we generated data for 5,000 measurement occasions, administering four items measuring a common momentary latent state, with two of these negatively worded. We note that the characteristics of the resultant attentive responses (stemming from a short, unidimensional scale with homogeneous items) pose rather challenging conditions to disentangle them from a residual state (Uglanova et al., 2025b). We varied the proportion of the residual state π 2 (.05; .10; .20) as well as the response behavior of observations within this state.

We considered three behavioral patterns characterizing item responses of the residual state: uniform random responding, midpoint responding, and strong observation-specific preferences-for slider position in the VAS format, and for response category in the Likert format-without regard to item content.

To generate attentive VAS responses, we used the Beta IRT model by Noel and Dauvier (2007), which assumes responses, re-scaled to values between 0 and 1, to be Beta-distributed. In this model, the expected value of a response is determined by the latent state θ it and item difficulty ν j , while the variance is governed by the dispersion parameter ζ j . Information on whether an item is positively (w j = 1) or negatively worded (w j = -1) is incorporated through the item wording indicator w j (Zhang, Domingue, et al., 2025):

For data generation, we set ν = (-1.00, 1.00, -0.75, 0.75) and ζ = (3.50, 4.00, 3.50, 4.00). These Note that the category characteristic curves for items worded in the same direction were highly similar. As expected, for the two positively worded items, the probability of endorsing higher response categories increased with higher levels on the latent momentary state, whereas for the two negatively worded items, it decreased. Table D1 displays means, standard deviations, and correlations of person attentiveness, log initial time expenditure, and log habitual decay. 6 From the mean log initial time expenditure and log habitual decay parameters, it can be concluded that, at the beginning of the study, participants typically required markedly longer to provide attentive responses (exp(µ ln(τ 1 ) ) = 0.89, implying that the average respondent required exp(0.89) ≈ 2.44 times longer than the attentive minimum to complete the EMA on their first attempt), but sped-up across measurement occasions (exp(µ ln(τ² ) ) = 0.97), indicating that the average respondents' deviations from the attentive minimum decreased by a factor of 0.97 with each subsequent measurement).

The Likert group had 4,187 measurement occasions nested in 66 participants, and the VAS group had 3,725 occasions nested in 58 participants. Of 84 possible measurement occasions, participants completed 63 on average in the Likert group and 64 in the VAS group (75% and 76%, respectively). The EMA survey of the study included a transdiagnostic psychopathology questionnaire described in Jover Martínez et al. (2024); we here make use of the total time participants required to respond to the questionnaire items. The questionnaire comprised 29 core items assessing, among others, mood, physical sensations, behaviors, and thoughts. An additional set of 39 items was presented only when triggered by specific responses to one of the core items. Note that such routings challenge the screen-time-based mixture modeling approach employed in Study II, as the number of presented items and, hence, the time required for completing the questionnaire varies across observations.
